glossary.definition: Combining lexical and semantic retrieval signals, often by fusing rankings rather than adding uncalibrated raw scores.
A rank aggregation method that adds 1/(k0 + rank) contributions for each result across multiple ranked lists.
A retrieval scoring approach that retains token-level vectors and aggregates token-to-token similarity, such as MaxSim.
A more expensive relevance model applied to a bounded candidate set after initial retrieval.
Using entity and relation edges to discover connected evidence, while rechecking ACLs on every retrieved evidence chunk.
The effective time interval during which a document version or evidence chunk is considered valid.
Metadata linking an answer span to an immutable source version, page, chunk and character/token offsets.
A candidate index queried alongside the current index for quality comparison without serving user-visible results.
Reducing the evidence context to fit a token budget while preserving supported source facts and citation lineage.

explanation.problem: A high vector similarity score does not prove relevance, freshness or authorization. Production retrieval systems fail when ACL filters run after top-k, cache keys omit tenant or policy versions, graph expansion follows unauthorized edges, compression loses source offsets, or an index is promoted without quality evidence. The goal is not just to retrieve similar text; it is to retrieve the best authorized, current and citable evidence within a measurable budget.
explanation.plainLanguage:
Begin with access, not embeddings. Resolve the user on the server and construct an access context containing tenant, subject, roles, allowed document set and as-of time. Filter the corpus using those predicates before ranking. If you rank first and filter later, unauthorized documents can occupy the top-k slots, affect result counts and leak information through scores or timing. Every secondary path—reranking, graph expansion, parent chunks and cache hits—must preserve the same access policy.

Different retrieval methods solve different problems. Lexical retrieval is good at exact words, IDs, dates and rare terms. Dense retrieval finds semantically related passages even when wording differs, but can miss exact identifiers or retrieve a plausible yet wrong paragraph. Hybrid retrieval combines their rankings. Reciprocal Rank Fusion is useful when raw lexical and vector scores are not calibrated to the same scale: each result contributes 1/(k0+rank) from each ranked list. Multi-vector or late-interaction methods keep more token-level representation. A MaxSim-style score finds, for each query token vector, the best matching document token vector and aggregates those matches. It can improve fine-grained relevance at higher storage and compute cost.

Query planning identifies multiple information needs. Split a question into sub-queries, route exact identifier searches to lexical retrieval, use dense or hybrid retrieval for semantic questions, and request freshness-aware filtering for words such as current, latest or effective. Rerank only a bounded authorized candidate set. Graph retrieval can connect a policy to its exception or approval record, but a graph edge is a navigation hint, not a permission grant. Recheck the target evidence chunk's tenant, ACL and temporal validity before adding it.

Context engineering is more than concatenating top-k chunks. Preserve document ID, immutable version, page, section, source offsets and retrieval metadata. Deduplicate overlapping passages, retain parent context where a child chunk needs it, order evidence by relevance and coverage, and compress only by selecting faithful source spans. Do not invent a shorter paraphrase and reuse the original citation as if the source said those words. If no authorized evidence fits the budget, abstain or ask for clarification.

Retrieval caches are security-sensitive. Include tenant, subject or ACL scope, roles, allowed documents, freshness/as-of policy, model version, embedding version, index version and authorization policy version in the cache key. Invalidate on document deletion, permission changes, version updates and index promotion. A cache hit must not bypass current authorization.

For index migration, build a candidate in parallel, shadow the same authorized queries, compare result overlap and task quality by tenant and query slice, validate embedding dimensions and citation lineage, and require predeclared thresholds before promotion. Keep the old index compatible for rollback. A successful indexing job alone is not proof of a safe migration.
explanation.mentalModel: Verified identity → access context → query plan → ACL/tenant/time filter → authorized candidates → lexical/dense/multi-vector retrieval → fusion/rerank → ACL-checked graph expansion → faithful context compression → versioned citations → grounded answer or abstention.
limitations: Synthetic vectors and scoring functions teach mechanics but do not represent a real embedding model or production vector database benchmark.
RRF is a rank aggregation method, not a calibrated probability or guarantee of relevance.
Late interaction can improve token-level matching but increases storage, memory and query-time cost.
A graph edge may be stale or poisoned; every linked evidence chunk needs provenance, freshness and authorization checks.
Source-preserving sentence selection is not a general semantic compressor and may omit important context; evaluate faithfulness and coverage.
A cache key reduces cross-scope collisions but does not replace reauthorization or invalidation on data/ACL changes.
Shadow overlap is one migration signal; it must be combined with labeled relevance, citation correctness, freshness, latency and cost gates.
explanation.everydayAnalogy: A librarian first checks whether a visitor is allowed into a restricted archive, then searches the catalog using exact titles and related concepts. A research assistant may follow a reference to another book, but the second book still needs its own access check. A summary card keeps the book edition and page number so the reader can verify the quotation.
explanation.mathMadeSimple: For a query, lexical ranks are [A,B,C] and dense ranks are [B,C,A]. With k0=60, RRF(A)=1/61+1/63, RRF(B)=1/62+1/61, RRF(C)=1/63+1/62. B receives the highest fused score. RRF combines rank evidence without assuming raw BM25 and cosine scores share a common scale.
explanation.productionImpact: Measure Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR/NDCG, citation correctness, faithfulness, abstention, freshness, p95 latency and cost by tenant and query slice. Apply ACL predicates before top-k; use ACL-aware cache keys and reauthorization; pin embedding/index versions; preserve citation offsets; test graph traversal and reranker inputs; and gate index promotion on shadow quality and rollback readiness.

useCase.scenario: A multi-tenant policy assistant answers questions about current retention rules, exceptions and approval paths. It combines lexical and dense retrieval, fuses rankings, reranks authorized candidates, expands a policy graph, compresses evidence into a limited context and returns citations with exact document versions and page offsets.

constraints: Unauthorized or stale chunks are filtered before scoring and top-k.
Graph edges and cached evidence never grant access.
Context compression preserves exact source text and citation lineage.

Index promotion requires shadow quality evidence and a rollback target.

Cache key and index version metadata
useCase.successMetric: No unauthorized chunk enters the ranker or context; retrieval strategy returns relevant authorized evidence; citations resolve to source version/page/offset; context fits the token budget; cache keys isolate ACL/version changes; and a low-quality candidate index cannot be promoted.

trustBoundaries: User query and retrieved text are untrusted input.
Identity and tenant scope come from verified server context.
Vector scores and graph edges do not grant authorization.
Reranker output cannot widen the authorized candidate set.
Cache hits are reauthorized against current policy and data versions.
Citation metadata is preserved from the source parser, not generated by the model.
failurePaths: ACL predicate omitted before top-k: fail security acceptance and block retrieval.
Stale or expired document version: filter before ranking and invalidate cache.
Embedding dimension mismatch: reject index/query compatibility and route to known-good version.
Graph neighbor ACL denial: omit the neighbor and emit a safe audit reason.
Compression removes all supporting evidence: abstain rather than fabricate.
Cache key misses policy/index version: invalidate and recompute.
Candidate index quality below threshold: remain in shadow and do not promote.

failures.name: Filter after top-k
failures.symptom: A tenant-B document displaces tenant-A evidence or appears in result metadata.
failures.rootCause: ACL is applied after vector or lexical top-k rather than in the candidate query.
failures.recovery: Push tenant/document ACL predicates into the retrieval query before ranking and verify with a ranker spy.
failures.regressionTest: Inject a higher-scoring cross-tenant chunk and assert it never appears in last_ranked_candidates.

failures.name: Dense score misses exact identifier
failures.symptom: A semantically similar passage outranks the exact policy ID or product code.
failures.rootCause: Dense embeddings smooth rare identifiers and exact strings.
failures.recovery: Add lexical retrieval and fuse rankings with RRF; preserve exact identifier filters.
failures.regressionTest: Use a rare identifier query and assert lexical/hybrid retrieves the exact source.

failures.name: Graph ACL bypass
failures.symptom: A related document from another tenant enters context through graph traversal.
failures.rootCause: The seed chunk was authorized but target evidence ACL was not rechecked.
failures.recovery: Treat edges as navigation only and authorize every target evidence chunk.
failures.regressionTest: Add cross-tenant graph evidence and assert it is omitted.

failures.name: Citation lineage lost during compression
failures.symptom: The generated context cannot be traced to an immutable document version/page/offset.
failures.rootCause: Compression returns free-form paraphrases or drops source metadata.
failures.recovery: Select exact source spans and carry citation metadata through every transformation.
failures.regressionTest: Assert compressed evidence is a source substring and citation fields remain unchanged.

failures.name: Cross-tenant cache collision
failures.symptom: A user receives a cached result created under another tenant or ACL.
failures.rootCause: Cache key omits tenant, subject, allowed docs or policy version.
failures.recovery: Bind cache identity to full access and model/index/policy version context and reauthorize hits.
failures.regressionTest: Change tenant, ACL, index or policy and assert cache keys differ.

failures.name: Unsafe index promotion
failures.symptom: New index is promoted despite losing important authorized results.
failures.rootCause: Promotion depends on indexing success or aggregate overlap alone.
failures.recovery: Shadow representative queries, evaluate slices and require predeclared quality thresholds with rollback.
failures.regressionTest: Low overlap or a failing slice blocks promotion.

scenarioQuiz.question: A cross-tenant document has the highest cosine similarity. When must it be removed?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Authorization must constrain the candidate set before ranking. Post-ranking filtering can leak information and displace valid evidence.

scenarioQuiz.question: Why use reciprocal-rank fusion for lexical and dense retrieval?
options: It proves a result is correct
It combines rankings without assuming raw scores share a scale
It removes the need for ACL filters
scenarioQuiz.explanation: RRF aggregates rank positions and is useful when BM25-like and cosine scores are not calibrated to a common numeric scale.

scenarioQuiz.question: A graph edge points from an authorized policy chunk to a restricted exception document. What should happen?
options: Include it because the seed was authorized
Recheck the target evidence ACL and omit it if unauthorized
Treat the edge as an access grant
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Graph edges are navigation hints, not permissions. Every evidence chunk must independently pass tenant, ACL and freshness checks.

scenarioQuiz.question: Which dimensions should affect a retrieval cache key?
options: Query, tenant/ACL, freshness, model, embedding, index and policy versions
scenarioQuiz.explanation: A cache key must isolate security scope and every version dimension that can change retrieval semantics. Cache hits still require reauthorization.

references.title: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT

codeWalkthrough.explanation: Resolve tenant, document ACL, subject/role and temporal validity before calculating any lexical or vector score. The rejected count is safe aggregate evidence, not the identities of unauthorized documents.
Dense similarity ranks semantic proximity but is not an authorization decision or calibrated probability of answer correctness.
RRF contributes a bounded rank-based score from each retrieval list and combines heterogeneous ranking signals without adding uncalibrated raw scores.
For each query token vector, compute its maximum similarity to document token vectors and aggregate those maxima. This retains fine-grained matching at greater storage/compute cost.

codeWalkthrough.lines: evidence = graph_expand(seed_hits, edges, chunks_by_id, access, max_hops)
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Graph traversal is bounded and each target evidence chunk passes the same authorization check. A relationship edge never grants access.

codeWalkthrough.lines: Citation(doc_id, version, page, start_offset, end_offset, chunk_id)
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Citation lineage travels with the exact selected source span, allowing a downstream answer to be verified against the immutable source version.

codeWalkthrough.lines: retrieval_cache_key(... tenant, ACL, model, embedding, index, policy ...)
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Cache identity changes whenever access scope, freshness or retrieval semantics change. Cache hits still need current authorization.
An index candidate remains in shadow until measured query overlap meets the predeclared gate. Production promotion also needs relevance, freshness, citation, latency and cost evidence.
